label: twist-mult
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{twist-mult}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $\, (S, \cdot)$ a semigroup $\, \Gamma$-graded by $\phi : S \setminus\{0\} \to \Gamma$, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $S$. Define a binary operation $*$ on $S$ via 
\[s * t := s \tau_{\alpha}(t),\] 
for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\alpha}$, and $t \in S$. Then $\, (S,*)$ is a semigroup, $\, \Gamma$-graded by $\phi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \Gamma$, $r \in S_{\alpha}$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S_{\gamma}$. Since $\tau_{\alpha}(s) \in S_{\beta}$,
\[r*(s*t) = r\tau_{\alpha}(s\tau_{\beta}(t)) = r\tau_{\alpha}(s)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (r*s)*t.\]
Thus $*$ is associative, and hence $(S,*)$ is a semigroup. If $s*t \neq 0$, then $s \tau_{\beta}(t) \neq 0$, and so
\[\phi(s*t) = \phi(s \tau_{\beta}(t)) = \phi(s)\phi(\tau_{\beta}(t)) = \beta\gamma = \phi(s)\phi(t),\]
since $\tau_{\beta}$ is graded. Thus $\phi$ defines a grading on $(S,*)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup, $\tau$ a Zhang twist on $S$, and $*$ as in Lemma~\ref{twist-mult}. We denote the semigroup $(S,*)$ by $S^{\tau}$, and refer to it as the \emph{(Zhang) twisting of $S$ by $\tau$}, or, more simply, as a \emph{twisted} semigroup.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The above definition of ``twisting" is clearly not left-right symmetric. Analogously to~\cite[Definition 4.1]{Zhang}, one can define a \emph{left Zhang twist} $
u$ on a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup $S$ to be a collection $\{
u_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$, where $
u_{\alpha} : S 	o S$ is a graded bijection for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$, and
\[
u_{\alpha}(
u_{ eta}(s)t) = 
u_{ eta\alpha}(s)
u_{\alpha}(t)\]
for all $\alpha,  eta \in \Gamma$, $s \in S$, and $t \in S_{ eta}$. Then one can show that, in this situation, the operation $s * t := 
u_{\alpha}(s)t$ ($\alpha \in \Gamma$, $s \in S$, $t \in S_{\alpha}$), turns $(S,*)$ into a semigroup $\prescript{
u}{}S$, with the same grading.

It is easy to see that a \emph{left twisting} of $S$, as above, corresponds to a twisting of $S^{\mathrm{op}}$, the opposite semigroup of $S$, graded by $\Gamma^{\mathrm{op}}$, the opposite group of $\Gamma$, and vice versa. So a separate theory of left twistings is unnecessary. Moreover, using the same argument as in~\cite[Theorem 4.3]{Zhang}, one can show that given a Zhang twist $	au = \{	au_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ on $S$, letting $
u_{\alpha}(s) = 	au_{ eta\alpha}	au_{ eta}^{-1}(s)$ for all $\alpha,  eta \in \Gamma$ and $s \in S_{ eta}$, defines a left twisting $
u$ of $S$, such that $\prescript{
u}{}S \cong S^{	au}$ as graded semigroups.

label: alg-eg
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{alg-eg}
Let $\Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup, and $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{gr}}(S)$ the group of graded semigroup automorphisms of $S$. Suppose that $\tau : \Gamma \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{gr}}(S)$ is a homomorphism, and let $\tau_{\alpha} := \tau(\alpha)$ for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Then for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S$ we have 
\[\tau_{\alpha}(s\tau_{\beta}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha}(s)\tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha}(s)\tau_{\alpha \beta}(t),\]
since $\tau(\alpha)\tau(\beta) = \tau(\alpha\beta)$. Therefore $\{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is an algebraic Zhang twist on $S$.

label: aut-eg
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{aut-eg}
Let $S$ be a $\mathbb Z$-graded semigroup, where $\mathbb Z$ denotes the group of the integers, and let $\psi : S \rightarrow S$ be a graded automorphism. Then $\tau(n) := \psi^n$ gives a homomorphism $\tau : \mathbb Z \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{gr}}(S)$, and so $\{\psi^n \mid n \in \mathbb Z\}$ is an algebraic Zhang twist on $S$, by Remark~\ref{alg-eg}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $X$ be a set, and let $F=\langle X \rangle$ denote either the free semigroup or the free commutative semigroup (with zero) generated by $X$. Letting $F_n$ denote the subset of $F$ consisting of words of length $n$ in the generators, together with $0$, we obtain a $\mathbb Z$-grading $F=\bigcup_{i\geq 0} F_n$, with support $\mathbb N$ (the set of the natural numbers). Any bijection $f : X \to X$ can be extended to a graded automorphism $\psi_f : F \rightarrow F$, via $\psi_f(0) := 0$, and $\psi_f(x_{1} \cdots x_{n}) := f(x_{1}) \cdots f(x_{n})$ for all $x_{1}, \dots, x_{n} \in X$. Then $\psi_f$ can be used to construct a Zhang twist on $F$, as in Remark~\ref{aut-eg}.

Now consider the particular case where $F$ is the free commutative semigroup generated by $\{x,y\}$. Let $f : \{x,y\} \rightarrow \{x,y\}$ be defined by $f(x) := y$ and $f(y) := x$, extend $f$ to an automorphism $\psi_f : F \rightarrow F$, as above, and let $\tau := \{\psi_f^n \mid n \in \mathbb Z\}$ be the resulting Zhang twist on $F$. Then in $F^{\tau}$ we have $x * y = x \psi_f(y) = x^2$ and $y * x = y \psi_f(x) = y^2$. So $F^{\tau}$ is not commutative, and therefore not isomorphic to $F$. It is also not hard to see that $F^{\tau}$ is not isomorphic to the free semigroup on two generators.

label: ring-twist
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ring-twist}
Recall that given a group $\Gamma$, a ring $A$ is $\Gamma$-\emph{graded} if $A = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Gamma} A_{\alpha}$, where the $A_{\alpha}$ are additive subgroups of $A$, and $A_{\alpha} A_{\beta} \subseteq A_{\alpha \beta}$ for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$ (with $A_{\alpha} A_{\beta}$ denoting the set of all sums of elements of the form $ab$, with $a \in A_{\alpha}$ and $b \in A_{\beta}$). For any $\Gamma$-graded ring $A$, letting $S:= \bigcup_{\alpha \in \Gamma} A_{\alpha}$ gives a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup, under multiplication. 

Now let $K$ be a commutative unital ring, $\Gamma$ a group, and $A$ a $\Gamma$-graded $K$-algebra. According to~\cite[Definition 2.1]{Zhang}, a \emph{(Zhang) twisting system $\tau$ on $A$} is a collection $\{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$, where $\tau_{\alpha} : A \to A$ is a $K$-linear graded bijection for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$, and
\[\tau_{\alpha}(a\tau_{\beta}(b)) = \tau_{\alpha}(a)\tau_{\alpha \beta}(b)\]
for all $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \Gamma$, $a \in A_{\beta}$, and $b \in A_{\gamma}$. Clearly, in this situation, restricting each $\tau_{\alpha}$ to $S := \bigcup_{\alpha \in \Gamma} A_{\alpha}$ leads to a Zhang twist, in the sense of Definition~\ref{twist-def}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Let $\Gamma$ be a group, $K$ a commutative ring, $A = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Gamma} A_{\alpha}$ a $\Gamma$-graded $K$-algebra, and $S := \bigcup_{\alpha \in \Gamma} A_{\alpha}$ (as in Example~\ref{ring-twist}). Suppose that $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a Zhang twist on $S$, such that each $\tau_{\alpha} : S \rightarrow S$ extends to a $K$-linear function $\tau_{\alpha} : A \to A$. Then it is easy to see that extending each $\tau_{\alpha}$ in that manner gives a twisting system on $A$, in the sense of~\cite[Definition 2.1]{Zhang}, and every twisting system on $A$ arises this way.

label: twist-id-elt
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) The first claim follows immediately from the hypothesis that $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a graded bijection of $S$, for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$, and the fact that $0$ is the unique element of $S$ common to every component $S_{\beta}$. The second claim is an easy consequence of the first.

\smallskip

(2) Suppose that $S$ is a monoid and $\tau_{\varepsilon}(1) = 1$, and let $s \in S$. Then
\[\tau_{\varepsilon}(\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(1\cdot \tau_{\varepsilon}(s)) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(1)\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(s).\]
Since $\tau_{\varepsilon}$ is a bijection, this implies that $\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = s$.

The converse is tautological.

\smallskip

(3) Suppose that $S$ is a monoid, and let $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Then, using (3) in Lemma~\ref{id-lem}, 
\[1 = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(1) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(1 \cdot \tau_{\alpha}(1)) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(1)\tau_{\varepsilon}(\tau_{\alpha\varepsilon}^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(1)) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(1)\tau_{\varepsilon}(1).\]

\smallskip

(4) Suppose that $S$ is an inverse semigroup, and $\tau_{\varepsilon}(u) = u$ for all $u \in E(S)$. Let $s \in S$, and set $u := \tau_{\varepsilon}(s)\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)^{-1} \in E(S) \subseteq S_{\varepsilon}$. Then
\[\tau_{\varepsilon}(\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(u\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)) =  \tau_{\varepsilon}(u)\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = u\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(s),\]
and so $\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = s$, given that $\tau_{\varepsilon}$ is a bijection.

The converse is tautological.

label: id-fix
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{id-fix}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroup, and $\tau$ a Zhang twist on $S$. Then there is a Zhang twist $\sigma$ on $S$ such that $\sigma_{\varepsilon}(s) = s$ for all $s \in S$, and $S^{\tau} \cong S^{\sigma}$, via a graded isomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$, choose $\gamma \in \Gamma$, and define $\sigma_{\alpha} := \tau_{\gamma\alpha}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}$ for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Then $\sigma_{\varepsilon} (s) = \tau_{\gamma}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(s) = s$ for all $s\in S$, and clearly $\sigma_{\alpha} : S \to S$ is a graded bijection for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Now, let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S$. Then, using (2) in Lemma~\ref{id-lem}, 
\begin{multline*}
\sigma_{\alpha}(s\sigma_{\beta}(t)) = \tau_{\gamma\alpha}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(s\tau_{\gamma\beta}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(t)) = \tau_{\gamma\alpha}(\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(s)\tau_{\beta}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(t))\\
= \tau_{\gamma\alpha}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(s)\tau_{\gamma\alpha\beta}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}(t) = \sigma_{\alpha}(s)\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(t).
\end{multline*}
Hence $\sigma = \{\sigma_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a Zhang twist on $S$.

Finally, let $\star$ denote the multiplication in $S^{\sigma}$. Then for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\alpha}$, and $t \in S$,
\[\tau_{\gamma}(s*t) = \tau_{\gamma}(s \tau_{\alpha}(t)) = \tau_{\gamma}(s) \tau_{\gamma\alpha}(t) = \tau_{\gamma}(s) \tau_{\gamma\alpha}\tau_{\gamma}^{-1}\tau_{\gamma}(t) = \tau_{\gamma}(s) \sigma_{\alpha}(\tau_{\gamma}(t)) = \tau_{\gamma}(s) \star \tau_{\gamma}(t).\]
It follows that $\tau_{\gamma} : S^{\tau} \to S^{\sigma}$ is an isomorphism, and it is graded, by Lemma~\ref{twist-mult}.

label: inverse-twist
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Clearly $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1} : S \to S$ is a graded bijection for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Also, for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S$, using (3) in Lemma~\ref{id-lem} gives
\[\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s * \tau_{\beta}^{-1}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(st) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s)\tau_{\beta}\tau_{\alpha \beta}^{-1}(t)  = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s) * \tau_{\alpha \beta}^{-1}(t),\]
where $*$ is the multiplication in $S^{\tau}$. Hence $\tau^{-1}$ is a Zhang twist on $S^{\tau}$.

\smallskip

(2) As above, $\tau_{\alpha}\sigma_{\alpha} : S \to S$ is certainly a graded bijection for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Now, for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S$, we have
\begin{multline*}
\tau_{\alpha}\sigma_{\alpha} (s\tau_{\beta}\sigma_{\beta} (t)) = \tau_{\alpha}\sigma_{\alpha} (s*\sigma_{\beta} (t)) = \tau_{\alpha} (\sigma_{\alpha}(s)*\sigma_{\alpha\beta} (t))\\
= \tau_{\alpha} (\sigma_{\alpha}(s)\tau_{\beta}\sigma_{\alpha\beta} (t)) = \tau_{\alpha} \sigma_{\alpha}(s)\tau_{\alpha\beta}\sigma_{\alpha\beta} (t),
\end{multline*}
where $*$ is the multiplication in $S^{\tau},$ and so $\tau\sigma$ is a Zhang twist on $S$. Next, let $\star$, respectively $\bullet$, denote the multiplication in $S^{\tau\sigma}$, respectively $(S^{\tau})^{\sigma}$. Then for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\alpha}$, and $t \in S$,
\[s \star t = s\tau_{\alpha}\sigma_{\alpha}(t) = s*\sigma_{\alpha}(t) = s \bullet t.\]
It follows that $(S^{\tau\sigma}, \star) = ((S^{\tau})^{\sigma},\bullet)$.

label: idempt-lem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{idempt-lem}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded inverse semigroup, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $S$, such that $\tau_{\varepsilon}(u)=u$ for all $u \in E(S)$. Then $E(S) = \tau_{\alpha}(E(S)) = E(S^{\tau})$ for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $u \in S$ and $\alpha \in \Gamma$. If $u \in E(S)$, then $u \in S_{\varepsilon}$, and so, using the hypothesis on $\tau_{\varepsilon}$, gives
\[u*u = u \tau_{\varepsilon}(u) = u^2 = u\]
and $u \in E(S^{\tau})$. Additionally, if $u \in E(S)$, then
\[u = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(u^2) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(u\tau_{\varepsilon}(u)) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(\tau_{\alpha}(u)\tau_{\alpha}(u)),\]
which implies that $\tau_{\alpha}(u) = \tau_{\alpha}(u)^2$. Thus $\tau_{\alpha}(E(S)) \subseteq E(S) \subseteq E(S^{\tau})$.

Next, suppose that $\tau_{\alpha}(u) \in E(S)$. Then $\tau_{\alpha}(u) \in S_{\varepsilon}$, and so
\[\tau_{\alpha}(u) = \tau_{\alpha}(u)\tau_{\alpha}(u) = \tau_{\alpha}(u\tau_{\varepsilon}(u)) = \tau_{\alpha}(u^2).\]
Since $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a bijection, this means that $u = u^2$, and so $u \in E(S)$. Since $\tau_{\alpha}(E(S)) \subseteq E(S)$, using once again the fact that $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a bijection on $S$, we conclude that $E(S) = \tau_{\alpha}(E(S))$.

Finally, suppose that $u \in E(S^{\tau})$. Then $u \in S_{\varepsilon}^{\tau} = S_{\varepsilon}$, and so
\[u = u*u = u \tau_{\varepsilon}(u) = u^2.\]
Thus, $u \in E(S)$, and therefore $E(S) = E(S^{\tau})$.

label: twist-reg
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}, it suffices to prove only the forward implication of each statement. Moreover, each of the properties in question is preserved by isomorphism, and so, by Proposition~\ref{id-fix}, we may assume that $\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)=s$ for all $s \in S$. 

\smallskip

(1) Suppose that $S$ is regular, and let $\alpha \in \Gamma$ and $s \in S_{\alpha}$ be arbitrary. Then there exists $t \in S$ such that $sts=s$, where, necessarily, $st \in E(S) \subseteq S_{\varepsilon}$. Therefore
\[(s* \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(t))*s = (s\tau_{\alpha}\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(t))*s = st\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = sts = s,\]
and so $S^{\tau}$ is regular.

\smallskip

(2) Suppose that $S$ is an inverse semigroup. Then idempotents in $S$ commute--see, e.g.,~\cite[Theorem 5.1.1]{Howie}. Now, let $u,v \in E(S^{\tau})$. Then $u,v \in E(S)$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}, and hence
\[u*v = u \tau_{\varepsilon}(v) = uv = vu = v \tau_{\varepsilon}(u) = v*u.\]
Since $S^{\tau}$ is regular, by (1), and has commuting idempotents, it is an inverse semigroup, by~\cite[Theorem 5.1.1]{Howie}.
head: environment

label: npt
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{twist-reg}(1),
\[(s* \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}))*s = (s\tau_{\alpha}\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}))*s = ss^{-1}\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = ss^{-1}s = s.\]
It follows that $s_{\tau}^{*}:=\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})*s*\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})$ is the unique inner inverse of $s$ in $S^{\tau}$. (In any inverse semigroup, if $xyx = x$ for some elements $x$ and $y$, then also $x(yxy)x=x$ and $(yxy)x(yxy)=yxy$.) Now, since $s^{-1} \in S_{\alpha^{-1}}$,
\[s_{\tau}^{*} = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})*(s\tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}) * ss^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(ss^{-1})\]
Applying (2) in Lemma~\ref{id-lem} gives
\[s_{\tau}^{*} = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}\tau_{\varepsilon}(ss^{-1})) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}ss^{-1}) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}).\]

\smallskip

(2) Suppose that $\tau$ is algebraic. Then $\tau_{\alpha}\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s^{-1}) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(s^{-1}) = s^{-1}$, and therefore $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s^{-1})$. Since $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}$ is, by hypothesis, a semigroup automorphism, it follows that $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1}) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s)^{-1}$.

\smallskip

(3) Suppose that $s \leq t$. Then $s = ut$ for some $u \in E(S)$. Hence
\[u*t = u\tau_{\varepsilon}(t) = ut = s.\]
Since $u \in E(S^{\tau})$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}, we conclude that $s \leq^{\tau} t$. Thus $\leq$ is contained in $\leq^{\tau}$. The opposite inclusion follows from Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}.

\smallskip

(4) Suppose that $r \leq t$, and write $r = ut$ for some $u \in E(S)$. Then
\[\tau_{\alpha}(r) = \tau_{\alpha}(ut) = \tau_{\alpha}(u\tau_{\varepsilon}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha}(u)\tau_{\alpha}(t).\]
Hence $\tau_{\alpha}(r) \leq \tau_{\alpha}(t)$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}.

Conversely, suppose that $\tau_{\alpha}(r) \leq \tau_{\alpha}(t)$. Then, using Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}, we can write $\tau_{\alpha}(r) = \tau_{\alpha}(u)\tau_{\alpha}(t)$ for some $u \in E(S)$. Hence
\[\tau_{\alpha}(r) = \tau_{\alpha}(u)\tau_{\alpha}(t) = \tau_{\alpha}(u\tau_{\varepsilon}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha}(ut).\]
Since $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a bijection, we conclude that $r \leq t$.

\smallskip

(5) We have
\[\tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha}(tt^{-1}t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha}(tt^{-1}\tau_{\varepsilon}(t))\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha}(tt^{-1})\tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}.\]
Since $\tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1} \in E(S)$, we see that
\begin{equation} \label{ineq-eq}
\tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1} \leq \tau_{\alpha}(tt^{-1}).
\end{equation}

To show the opposite inequality we note that, by Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}(1), $\tau^{-1} = \{\tau_{\alpha}^{-1} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a Zhang twist on $S^{\tau}$. Hence, substituting $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}$ for $\tau_{\alpha}$ in equation~(\ref{ineq-eq}) gives
\[\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(t)\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(t)^{-1} \leq^{\tau} \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(tt^{-1}).\]
Further substituting $\tau_{\alpha}(t)$ for $t$ we obtain
\[tt^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(\tau_{\alpha}(t))\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(\tau_{\alpha}(t))^{-1} \leq^{\tau} \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(\tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}),\]
and, by (3), also
\[tt^{-1} \leq \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(\tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}).\]
Taking $\tau_{\alpha}$ of both sides, by (4), we conclude that $\tau_{\alpha}(tt^{-1}) \leq \tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}$.

\smallskip

(6) Let $s_{\tau}^{*}$ and $t_{\tau}^{*}$ denote the inner inverses of $s$ and $t$ in $S^{\tau}$, respectively. Then, by (1),
\[s*t_{\tau}^{*} = s\tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(t^{-1})) = st^{-1}.\] 
Similarly,
\[\tau_{\alpha}(s_{\tau}^{*}*t) = \tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s^{-1})) \tau_{\alpha\alpha^{-1}}(t) = s^{-1}\tau_{\varepsilon}(t) = s^{-1}t.\]
Thus, if $s$ and $t$ are compatible in $S$, then they are compatible in $S^{\tau}$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem} and the hypothesis that $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a bijection. Likewise, if $s$ and $t$ are orthogonal in $S$, then they are orthogonal in $S^{\tau}$, by Lemma~\ref{twist-id-elt}(1). The converses of these statements follow from Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}.

title: Proof
body_md:
First, note that, by Lemma~\ref{twist-mult} and Proposition~\ref{twist-reg}(2), $S^{\tau}$ is a $\Gamma$-graded inverse semigroup. Also, by Proposition~\ref{id-fix}, we may assume that $\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)=s$ for all $s \in S$. 

\smallskip

(1) This follows from Lemma~\ref{npt}(3).

\smallskip

(2) By Lemma~\ref{npt}(6), for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ a pair of elements of $S_{\alpha} = S_{\alpha}^{\tau}$ is orthogonal in $S$ if and only if it is orthogonal in $S^{\tau}$. Thus such pairs have joins in $S$ if and only if they have joins in $S^{\tau}$, by Lemma~\ref{npt}(3). Also, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem} and Lemma~\ref{npt}(3), the lower semilattices $E(S)$ and $E(S^{\tau})$ are equal. Therefore $S$ satisfies the conditions in Definition~\ref{bool-def} if and only if $S^{\tau}$ does.

label: twist-invar
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{twist-invar}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroup, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $S$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$(1)$] $S$ is regular if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(2)$] $S$ is an inverse semigroup if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(3)$] $S$ is an inverse $\land$-semigroup if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(4)$] $S$ is a $\, \Gamma$-graded-Boolean inverse semigroup if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(5)$] $S$ is a $\, 0$-$E$-unitary inverse semigroup if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(6)$] $S$ is a band if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(7)$] $S$ is a monoid if and only if $S^{\tau}$ is.
\item[$(8)$] $S \setminus \{0\}$ is a group if and only if $S^{\tau} \setminus \{0\}$ is.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Statements (1)--(4) are proved in Propositions~\ref{twist-reg} and~\ref{bool-prop}. For each of the remaining statements, by Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}, it suffices to prove only the forward implication. Moreover, each of the properties in question is preserved by isomorphism, and so, by Proposition~\ref{id-fix}, we may assume that $\tau_{\varepsilon}(s)=s$ for all $s \in S$. 

\smallskip

(5) Suppose that $S$ is a $0$-$E$-unitary inverse semigroup. Then $S^{\tau}$ is an inverse semigroup, by $(2)$, and is $0$-$E$-unitary, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem} and Lemma~\ref{npt}(3).

\smallskip

(6) If $S$ is a band, then so is $S^{\tau}$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}.

\smallskip

(7) Suppose that $S$ is a monoid, and let $\alpha \in \Gamma$ and $s \in S_{\alpha}$ be arbitrary. By Lemma~\ref{twist-id-elt}(3), $1 = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(1)\tau_{\varepsilon}(1) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(1)$, and hence $\tau_{\alpha}(1)=1$. Therefore
\[1*s = 1\cdot \tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = 1\cdot s = s = s\cdot 1 = s\tau_{\alpha}(1) = s *1,\]
and so $S^{\tau}$ is a monoid.

\smallskip

(8) Suppose that $S\setminus \{0\}$ is a group (with identity $1$). Then, by (7) and its proof, $S^{\tau}$ is a monoid, with identity $1$. Also, by (2), $S^{\tau}$ is an inverse semigroup. Since $E(S) = \{0,1\}$, we have $E(S^{\tau}) = \{0,1\}$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}. Now, let $s \in S \setminus \{0\}$, and let $s_{\tau}^{*}$ denote the inner inverse of $s$ in $S^{\tau}$. Then $s*s_{\tau}^{*}$ and $s_{\tau}^{*}*s$ are nonzero idempotents in $S^{\tau}$, and hence $s*s_{\tau}^{*} = 1 = s_{\tau}^{*}*s$. Therefore $S^{\tau}\setminus \{0\}$ is a group.

title: Proof
body_md: We note that the degree-$0$ component $S_0$ is a submonoid of $S$. Since $ts=1$, the element $st$ is an idempotent. Hence the map $f$ is well-defined, and is an isomorphism of semigroups. The assignment $\phi:S_0[x,y,f]\rightarrow S$, where $\phi(x)=s$, $\phi(y)=t$, and $\phi(r)=r$ for all $r\in S_0$, satisfies the corner skew monoid relations (\ref{skewcornerla}), and induces a well-defined graded semigroup homomorphism. title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Suppose that $S$ is an inverse semigroup, and let $sf^i(1)x^i \in S[x,y,f]$ be an arbitrary element. An easy inductive argument shows that $x^iy^i = f^i(1)$ for all $i \in \mathbb N$. Since $f^i(1)$ is an idempotent, and since idempotents in $S$ commute, we have
\[(sf^i(1)x^i)(y^i f^i(1)s^{-1})(sf^i(1)x^i) = sf^i(1)s^{-1}sf^i(1)x^i = sf^i(1)x^i.\]
Likewise
\[(y^i f^i(1)s^{-1})(sf^i(1)x^i)(y^i f^i(1)s^{-1}) = y^i f^i(1)s^{-1},\]
and so $y^i f^i(1)s^{-1}$ is an inner inverse of $sf^i(1)x^i$. It is then easy to see that the only element of the form $y^j f^j(1)r$ that could play this role is $y^i f^i(1)s^{-1}$, and so $(sf^i(1)x^i)^{-1} = y^i f^i(1)s^{-1}$. Thus $S[x,y,f]$ is an inverse semigroup.

The converse is immediate. 

\smallskip

(2) Suppose that $S[x,y,f]$ is strongly graded. Since 
\[1\in S[x,y,f]_{0} = S[x,y,f]_1S[x,y,f]_{-1},\] 
$1=(rux)(yus)=rus$ for some $r,s \in S$. Thus for any $q\in S$ we have $q=q\cdot 1=qrus \in SuS$, and so $S=SuS$. 

The converse is also straightforward.

label: zhangskewsem
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{zhangskewsem}
Let $S[x,y,f]$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded corner skew monoid, $\psi$ a graded automorphism of $S[x,y,f]$, and $\tau := \{\psi^n \mid n \in \mathbb Z\}$ the corresponding algebraic Zhang twist on $S[x,y,f]$. Then $S[x,y,f]^{\tau} \cong S[x,y,gf]$, via a graded isomorphism, where $g:=\psi|_S$.
head: environment

label: gfyfhfh
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\psi : S[x,y,f] \rightarrow S[x,y,f]$ is a graded automorphism, it restricts to a homogeneous component bijection $\psi_i : S[x,y,f]_i \rightarrow S[x,y,f]_i$ for each $i \in \mathbb{Z}$. In particular, $g := \psi_0 \ (=\psi|_S)$ is a semigroup automorphism of $S$. Since $\psi$ is graded, necessarily
\[\psi(x)=sx \text{ and } \psi(y)=yt,\]
for some $s\in Su$ and $t\in uS$, where $f: S\rightarrow uSu$ and $f(1)=u$. The corner skew monoid relations (\ref{skewcornerla}) then imply that
\begin{align}\label{gfyfhfh}
& ts = u, \\\notag 
& st = g(u), \\ \notag
& s\,fg(r) = gf(r)\,s \text{ for all } r \in S, \\
& t\,gf(r) = fg(r)\,t  \text{ for all } r \in S. \notag
\end{align}
(For example, the third equality can be obtained from $\psi(xr) = \psi(f(r)x)$.)

For convenience, let $T : = S[x,y,f]^{\tau}$. Since for $y \in T_{-1}$ and $sx \in T_1$, we have
\[y*(sx)= y\,\psi^{-1}(sx) = yx = 1,\] 
by Lemma~\ref{chathapy}, $T \cong S[x,y,h]$ as graded semigroups, where
\begin{align}\label{djjhdd}
h : S &\longrightarrow (sx*y)\,S \, (sx*y),\\
r &\longmapsto sx * r * y. \notag
\end{align}
Note that 
\[sx*y= sx\psi(y)=sxyt=sut=st=g(u).\]
Using the relations (\ref{gfyfhfh}) and (\ref{skewcornerla}), we have, for all $r\in S$,
\begin{multline*}
h(r) = sx*r*y  = (sx)*(ry) = sx\,\psi(ry) = sx\,g(r)\,\psi(y) = sx\,g(r)\,yt = s \, fg(r) \, xyt \\ 
= s \, fg(r) \, ut = s \, fg(r) \,t  = gf(r) \, st = gf(r)g(u) = gf(r) = g(u)gf(r)g(u).
\end{multline*}
So (\ref{djjhdd}) takes the form 
\begin{align*}
h : S &\longrightarrow g(u) S g(u)\\
r &\longmapsto gf(r).
\end{align*}
Thus $S[x,y,f]^{\tau} \cong S[x,y,gf]$, via a graded isomorphism.

label: group-ext
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{group-ext}
If \[1\to N\to G\to \Gamma\to 1\] is a group extension with outer action $\Phi\colon \Gamma\to \mathrm{Out}(N)$, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a Zhang twist on $G$ such that $\tau_{\alpha}|_N=1_N$ for all $\alpha\in \Gamma$, then 
\[1\to N\to G^{\tau}\to \Gamma\to 1\] 
is an extension with outer action $\Phi$.  

Conversely, if 
\[1\to N\to G'\to\Gamma\to 1\] 
is a group extension with outer action $\Phi$, then $G'\cong G^\tau$ for a Zhang twist $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ on $G$, with $\tau_{\alpha}|_N=1_N$ for all $\alpha\in \Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $s\colon \Gamma\to G$ be a section with $s(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon$, and let $\varphi\colon \Gamma\to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ be as above, with $c$ the corresponding $2$-cocycle.   

First let $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ be a Zhang twist on $G$ such that $\tau_\alpha|_N=1_N$ for all $\alpha\in \Gamma$. Trivially 
\[1\to N\to G^{\tau}\to \Gamma\to 1\] 
is an extension. We check that it has outer action $\Phi$.  Indeed, if we use the same section $s$, then 
\[s(\gamma)\ast n\ast \tau_{\gamma}^{-1} (s(\gamma)^{-1})= s(\gamma)\tau_{\gamma}(n)s(\gamma)^{-1} = s(\gamma)ns(\gamma)^{-1}=\varphi_\gamma(n),\] 
by our assumption on $\tau$, along with Lemmas~\ref{twist-id-elt}(4) and~\ref{npt}(1).

For the converse, let $f$ be the $2$-cocycle corresponding to $G'$, with respect to a section $t$, with $t(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon$ and $t(\gamma)nt(\gamma)^{-1} = \varphi_\gamma(n)$.  Viewing $G$ as having underlying set $N\times \Gamma$, as above, define 
\[\tau_\alpha(n,\beta) := (n\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)),\beta).\]
Let us verify that $\tau$ is a Zhang twist. We shall use that $fc^{-1}\colon \Gamma\times \Gamma\to Z(N)$ is a $2$-cocycle.

We compute 
\begin{align*}
 \tau_\alpha((m,\beta)\tau_{\beta}(n,\gamma))&=\tau_{\alpha}((m,\beta)(n\varphi_\beta^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\beta,\gamma)),\gamma) \\ &= \tau_\alpha(m\varphi_\beta(n)fc^{-1}(\beta,\gamma)c(\beta,\gamma),\beta\gamma)\\ &= (m\varphi_\beta(n)fc^{-1}(\beta,\gamma)c(\beta,\gamma)\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta\gamma)),\beta\gamma)\\ &= (m\varphi_\beta(n)fc^{-1}(\beta,\gamma)\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta\gamma))c(\beta,\gamma),\beta\gamma),
\end{align*}
as $fc^{-1}$ takes values in $Z(N)$. On the other hand, using that $\varphi$ is an action on $Z(N)$ and that $fc^{-1}$ takes on values in the center, we have 
\begin{align*}
\tau_\alpha(m,\beta)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(n,\gamma) &= (m\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)),\beta)(n\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha\beta,\gamma)),\gamma) \\ &=(m\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)),\beta)(n\varphi_\beta^{-1}\varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha\beta,\gamma)),\gamma) \\ &= (m\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta))\varphi_\beta(n)\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha\beta,\gamma))c(\beta,\gamma),\beta\gamma) \\ &= (m\varphi_\beta(n)\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta))\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha\beta,\gamma))c(\beta,\gamma),\beta\gamma).
\end{align*}
Therefore, $\tau_\alpha((m,\beta)\tau_{\beta}(n,\gamma)) =\tau_\alpha(m,\beta)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(n,\gamma)$, by applying equation~\eqref{ga:cocycle.id} to $fc^{-1}$.
Note that, by equation~\eqref{ga:cocycle.normalized},
\[\tau_\alpha(n,\varepsilon) = (n\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\varepsilon)),\varepsilon) = (n,\varepsilon).\] 

Finally, we check that $G^\tau\cong G'$, where we view $G'$ as $N\times \Gamma$ with multiplication 
\[(m,\alpha)(n,\beta) := (m\varphi_\alpha(n)f(\alpha,\beta),\alpha\beta).\]  
Indeed, in $G^\tau$ we have 
\begin{align*}
(m,\alpha)\ast (n,\beta) &= (m,\alpha)\tau_\alpha(n,\beta) \\ &= (m,\alpha)(n\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(fc^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)),\beta) \\ &= (m\varphi_\alpha(n)f(\alpha,\beta)c(\alpha,\beta)^{-1} c(\alpha,\beta),\alpha\beta)
\\ &= (m\varphi_\alpha(n)f(\alpha,\beta),\alpha\beta)
\end{align*}
as required.

label: gp-eg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{gp-eg}
Let $i \geq 2$, $G := \mathbb Z_{i} \times \mathbb Z_{2}$, and $\Gamma := \mathbb Z_{2}$, viewed as additive groups. Then $G$ is $\Gamma$-graded by $\phi : G \to \Gamma$, where $\phi(m,n) := n$. Setting $N: = \mathbb Z_{i}$ gives the exact sequence 
\[0\to N\to G\to \Gamma\to 0.\]
Now, let $\tau_{0} : G \to G$ be the identity function, and define $\tau_{1} : G \to G$ by $\tau_{1}(m,0):= (m,0)$, and $\tau_{1}(m,1):= (m+1,1)$ for all $m \in \mathbb Z_{i}$. (So, in the notation of Theorem~\ref{group-ext}, $\tau_{0}|_N=1_N$ and $\tau_{1}|_N=1_N$.) Clearly, each of $\tau_{0}$ and $\tau_{1}$ is a graded bijection. It is easy to verify that
\[\tau_{\alpha}((m_1,n_1) + \tau_{\beta}((m_2,n_2))) = \tau_{\alpha}((m_1,n_1)) + \tau_{\alpha \beta}((m_2,n_2))\]
for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $(m_1,n_1) \in G_{\beta}$, and $(m_2,n_2) \in G$, by separately considering the cases where $n_1 = 0$, $n_2 = 0$, and $n_1=1=n_2$. Hence $\tau: = \{\tau_{0}, \tau_{1}\}$ is a Zhang twist on $G$. It is also easy to check that $G^{\tau}$ is generated by $(0,1)$, and is therefore isomorphic to $\mathbb Z_{2i}$. If $i \geq 3$, then $\tau_{1}$ is not a homomorphism, and so $\tau$ is not algebraic.

label: set-twist-mult
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{set-twist-mult}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroup, $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $S$, and $X$ a unitary pointed right $S$-set $\, \Gamma$-graded by $\phi : X \setminus \{0_X\} \to \Gamma$. Define an action of $S^\tau$ on $X$ via 
\[x * s := x \tau_{\alpha}(s),\] 
for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $x \in X_{\alpha}$, and $s \in S$. With respect to this action $X$ is a unitary pointed right $S^{\tau}$-set, which is $\, \Gamma$-graded by $\phi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $x \in X_{\alpha}$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S$. Then
\[(x*s)*t = (x \tau_{\alpha}(s))\tau_{\alpha\beta}(t) = x (\tau_{\alpha}(s)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(t)) = x (\tau_{\alpha}(s\tau_{\beta}(t)) = x* (s*t),\]
and so $X$ is a right $S^{\tau}$-set. Since $X$ is unitary as a right $S$-set, and each $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a bijection, $X$ is also unitary as a right $S^{\tau}$-set. Since $\tau_{\alpha}(0) = 0$ for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$, by Lemma~\ref{twist-id-elt}(1), we have $x*0 = x \tau_{\alpha}(0) = 0_X$ for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$ and $x \in X_{\alpha}$, and so $X$ is pointed as a right $S^{\tau}$-set, with the same zero element. 

Finally, suppose that $x*s \neq 0_X$. Then $x \tau_{\alpha}(s) \neq 0_X$, and so
\[\phi(x*s) = \phi(x \tau_{\alpha}(s)) = \phi (x)|\tau_{\alpha}(s)| = \phi (x)|s|,\]
since $\tau_{\alpha}$ is graded. Thus $X$ is $\Gamma$-graded by $\phi$, as a right $S^{\tau}$-set.

label: set-twist-def
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{set-twist-def}
Let $\Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup, $\tau$ a Zhang twist on $S$, and $X$ a $\Gamma$-graded right $S$-set. We denote the right $S^{\tau}$-set constructed from $X$ in Lemma~\ref{set-twist-mult} by $X^{\tau}$, and refer to it as the \emph{twisting of $X$ by $\tau$}.

label: cat-iso
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cat-iso}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroup, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $S$. Letting $\mathcal{F}(X) := X^{\tau}$, as in Definition~\ref{set-twist-def}, for each object $X$ in $\, \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$, and letting $\mathcal{F}(\psi) = \psi$ for each morphism $\psi$ in $\, \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$, defines an isomorphism of categories $\mathcal{F} : \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S \rightarrow \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau}$. Moreover, $\mathcal{F}(S(\alpha)) \cong S^{\tau}(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{set-twist-mult}, to conclude that $\mathcal{F}$ is well-defined, it suffices to check that given a morphism $\psi : X \rightarrow Y$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$, the function $\psi : X^{\tau} \rightarrow Y^{\tau}$ is a graded $S^{\tau}$-map. Thus let $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $x \in X_{\alpha}$, and $s \in S$. Then, using the hypothesis that $\psi$ is a graded $S$-map,
\[\psi(x*s) = \psi(x \tau_{\alpha}(s)) = \psi(x) \tau_{\alpha}(s) = \psi(x) * s,\]
and so $\psi$ is an $S^{\tau}$-map. Since the gradings on $S$ and $S^{\tau}$ coincide (see Lemma~\ref{set-twist-mult}), $\psi : X^{\tau} \rightarrow Y^{\tau}$ is also graded.

Next, let $\tau^{-1}:= \{\tau_{\alpha}^{-1} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$. Then, by Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}, $\tau^{-1}$ is a Zhang twist on $S^{\tau}$, and $ (S^{\tau})^{\tau^{-1}} = S^{\tau\tau^{-1}} = S$. Thus we can define a functor $\mathcal{G} : \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau} \rightarrow \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$ by letting $\mathcal{G}(X) = X^{\tau^{-1}}$ for each object $X$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau}$, and letting $\mathcal{G}(\psi) = \psi$ for each morphism $\psi$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau}$. This functor is well-defined, by the argument in the previous paragraph. Clearly $\mathcal{G} \circ \mathcal{F}(\psi) = \psi$ for every morphism $\psi$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$, and $\mathcal{F} \circ \mathcal{G}(\psi) = \psi$ for every morphism $\psi$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau}$. Hence, to conclude that $\mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism, it suffices to check that $\mathcal{G} \circ \mathcal{F}(X) = X$ for every object $X$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$ (and then $\mathcal{F} \circ \mathcal{G}(X) = X$ for every object $X$ in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau}$, by symmetry). Thus let $X$ be an object in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$, $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $x \in X_{\alpha}$, and $s \in S$. Denoting the action of $S^{\tau}$ on $X^{\tau}$ by $*$, and the action of $S$ on $(X^{\tau})^{\tau^{-1}}$ by $\star$, we have
\[x \star s = x* \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s) = x \tau_{\alpha}\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s) = xs.\]
Therefore $X = (X^{\tau})^{\tau^{-1}}$ as right $S$-sets, and so $\mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism.

To prove the final claim, let $\alpha \in \Gamma$ be arbitrary. Since $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}$ restricts to a bijection $S_{\beta} \to S_{\beta}$ for each $\beta \in \Gamma$, it induces a graded bijection $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}} : S^{\tau}(\alpha) \to S(\alpha)^{\tau}$. So it suffices to show that $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}$ is an $S^{\tau}$-map. Thus let $\beta \in \Gamma$, $s \in S_{\beta}$, and $t \in S$, and let $\star$ denote the $S^{\tau}$-action on $S(\alpha)^{\tau}$. Since the $S^{\tau}$-action $*$ on $S^{\tau}(\alpha)$ is the same as on $S^{\tau}$, and since $s \in S_{\alpha\alpha^{-1}\beta} = S(\alpha)_{\alpha^{-1}\beta}$, we have
\[\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s*t) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s\tau_{\beta}(t)) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s)\tau_{\alpha^{-1}\beta}(t) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s) \star t.\]
So $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}} : S^{\tau}(\alpha) \to \mathcal{F}(S(\alpha))$ is an isomorphism in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S^{\tau}$.

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $\Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup, $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $S$, and $X$ an object in $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$. For each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ define an action of $S^\tau$ on $X$ via 
\[x \star s := x\tau_{\alpha\beta}(s),\] 
for all $x \in X_{\beta}$ and $s \in S$. Then it is easy to see that with this action $X$ becomes a ($\Gamma$-graded unitary) right $S^\tau$-set, which we denote by $X^{\tau(\alpha)}$. 

Clearly $X^{\tau(\varepsilon)}=X^\tau$, as $\Gamma$-graded right $S^{\tau}$-sets. One can further check that 
\[X(\alpha)^{\tau(\beta)} = X^{\tau(\beta \alpha^{-1})} (\alpha),\] 
for all $\beta \in \Gamma$, as $\Gamma$-graded right $S^{\tau}$-sets.

label: delta-semi
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{delta-semi}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, let $S$ be a $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroup, and for all objects $X,Y$ in $\, \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$ let $\, \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)$ denote the set of morphisms $X \rightarrow Y$ in $\, \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S$. Also let 
\[\Delta(S) := \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in \Gamma} \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)\] 
denote the \emph{$0$-disjoint union} of the $\, \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$. $($That is, $\bigsqcup_{\alpha \in \Gamma} \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$ is the disjoint union of the sets $\, \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S) \setminus \{0\}$, together with a single zero function.$)$ 

Then $\Delta(S)$ is a $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroup, where $\Delta(S)_{\alpha} := \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$ for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Moreover, if $S$ is a monoid, then $S \cong \Delta(S)$, as $\, \Gamma$-graded semigroups.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $\phi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$, and $\psi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\beta^{-1}),S)$. Then, for all $\gamma \in \Gamma$, 
\[\psi(S((\alpha\beta)^{-1})_{\gamma}) = \psi(S(\beta^{-1})_{\alpha^{-1}\gamma}) \subseteq S_{\alpha^{-1}\gamma} = S(\alpha^{-1})_{\gamma}.\]
Thus we can view $\phi\psi$ as an element of $\mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S((\alpha\beta)^{-1}),S)$, upon interpreting $\psi$ as $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\psi)$. The fact that $\mathcal{T}_{\gamma^{-1}}\mathcal{T}_{\delta^{-1}} = \mathcal{T}_{(\gamma\delta)^{-1}}$, for all $\gamma, \delta \in \Gamma$, implies that this operation is associative. Moreover,
\[\Delta(S)_{\alpha}\Delta(S)_{\beta} = \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)\mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\beta^{-1}),S) \subseteq \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S((\alpha\beta)^{-1}),S) = \Delta(S)_{\alpha\beta},\]
and so $\Delta(S)$ is a $\Gamma$-graded semigroup.

Now suppose that $S$ is a monoid, and let $\alpha \in \Gamma$ and $\phi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$. Then $\phi(1) \in S_{\alpha}$, since $1 \in S(\alpha^{-1})_{\alpha}$. Moreover, for all $s \in S(\alpha^{-1})$ we have $\phi(s) = \phi(1\cdot s) = \phi(1)s$. So $\phi$ is uniquely determined by $\phi(1)$, and conversely each element of $S$ determines one in $\mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$. Thus letting $f(\phi) := \phi(1)$ defines a graded bijection $f: \Delta(S) \rightarrow S$. Also, for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $\phi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\alpha^{-1}),S)$, and $\psi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\beta^{-1}),S)$ we have
\[f(\phi)f(\psi) = \phi(1)\psi(1) = \phi(1 \cdot \psi(1)) = \phi(\psi(1)) = f(\phi\psi),\]
since $\phi$ is an $S$-map. Hence $S \cong \Delta(S)$, as $\Gamma$-graded semigroups.

label: iso-twist
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(1) \Rightarrow (2)$ Suppose that $\psi : T \rightarrow S^{\tau}$ is a graded isomorphism, where $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$. For each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ let $\phi_{\alpha} : = \tau_{\alpha}\psi$. Then for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $t_1 \in T_{\beta}$, and $t_2 \in T$,
\begin{multline*}
\phi_{\alpha}(t_1t_2) = \tau_{\alpha}\psi(t_1t_2) = \tau_{\alpha}(\psi(t_1)*\psi(t_2)) = \tau_{\alpha}(\psi(t_1)\tau_{\beta}\psi(t_2))\\
= \tau_{\alpha}(\psi(t_1))\tau_{\alpha\beta}\psi(t_2)) = \phi_{\alpha}(t_1)\phi_{\alpha\beta}(t_2).
\end{multline*}

\smallskip

$(2) \Rightarrow (1)$ Suppose that $\{\phi_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ satisfies the conditions in (2). Let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $s_1 \in S_{\beta}$, and $s_2 \in S$, and write $s_1 = \phi_{\alpha}(t_1)$ and $s_2 = \phi_{\alpha\beta}(t_2)$ for some $t_1 \in T_{\beta}$ and $t_2 \in T$. Then 
\[\phi_{\alpha}^{-1}(s_1s_2) = \phi_{\alpha}^{-1}(\phi_{\alpha}(t_1)\phi_{\alpha\beta}(t_2))  = \phi_{\alpha}^{-1}(\phi_{\alpha}(t_1t_2)) = t_1t_2 = \phi_{\alpha}^{-1}(s_1)\phi_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}(s_2).\]
Now, for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ let $\tau_{\alpha} := \phi_{\alpha}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}$. Then for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $s_1 \in S_{\beta}$, and $s_2 \in S$, we have
\[\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_1(\phi_{\beta}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_2))) = \phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_1)\phi_{\beta}^{-1}(\phi_{\beta}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_2)) = \phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_1)\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_2),\]
and so
\begin{multline*}
\tau_{\alpha}(s_1\tau_{\beta}(s_2)) = \phi_{\alpha}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_1\phi_{\beta}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_2)) = \phi_{\alpha}(\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_1)\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_2))\\
= \phi_{\alpha}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_1)\phi_{\alpha\beta}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(s_2) = \tau_{\alpha}(s_1)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(s_2).
\end{multline*}
Thus $\tau : = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a Zhang twist on $S$.

Finally, for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $t_1 \in T_{\beta}$, and $t_2 \in T$,
\[\phi_{\varepsilon}(t_1t_2) = \phi_{\varepsilon}(t_1)\phi_{\beta}(t_2) = \phi_{\varepsilon}(t_1)\phi_{\beta}\phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}\phi_{\varepsilon}(t_2) = \phi_{\varepsilon}(t_1)\tau_{\beta}\phi_{\varepsilon}(t_2) = \phi_{\varepsilon}(t_1)*\phi_{\varepsilon}(t_2),\]
and so $\phi_{\varepsilon}: T \rightarrow S^{\tau}$ is a graded isomorphism.

label: thmprehd6
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmprehd6}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, and let $S$ and $T$ be $\, \Gamma$-graded monoids. Then $T \cong S^{\tau}$ for some Zhang twist $\tau$ on $S$ if and only if there is an equivalence of categories $\mathcal{F} : \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S \rightarrow \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol T$, such that $\mathcal{F}(S(\alpha)) \cong T(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The forward implication follows from Theorem~\ref{cat-iso}. 

For the converse, suppose that $\mathcal{F} : \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol S \rightarrow \operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol T$ is an equivalence satisfying $\mathcal{F}(S(\alpha)) \cong T(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$. By Proposition~\ref{delta-semi}, it suffices to show that $\Delta(T) \cong \Delta(S)^{\tau}$, as graded semigroups, for some Zhang twist $\tau$ on $\Delta(S)$. 

For each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ let $\psi_{\alpha} : \mathcal{F}(S(\alpha)) \rightarrow T(\alpha)$ denote the graded isomorphism provided by hypothesis. Then $f_{\alpha\beta} (\theta) := \psi_{\alpha^{-1}}^{-1}\theta \psi_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}$ defines a graded bijection
\[f_{\alpha\beta} : \mathrm{Hom}_{T}(T(\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}),T(\alpha^{-1})) \rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{T}(\mathcal{F}(S(\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1})),\mathcal{F}(S(\alpha^{-1})))\]
for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$, where $\mathrm{Hom}_{T}$ refers to morphism sets in the category $\operatorname{\bf Gr-}\boldsymbol T$. Thus letting $\phi_{\alpha}(\rho) := \mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}f_{\alpha\beta}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\rho)$, for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$ and $\rho \in \mathrm{Hom}_{T}(T(\beta^{-1}), T)$, defines a graded bijection $\phi_{\alpha} : \Delta(T) \rightarrow \Delta(S)$--see the diagram below.
\[\xymatrix{\mathrm{Hom}_{T}(T(\beta^{-1}), T)\ar[d]^{\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}} & & \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\beta^{-1}), S)\\
 \mathrm{Hom}_{T}(T(\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}),T(\alpha^{-1}))\ar[rr]^{\mathcal{F}^{-1}f_{\alpha\beta}\ \ } & & \mathrm{Hom}_{S}(S(\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}),S(\alpha^{-1}))\ar[u]^{\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}}}\]
By Proposition~\ref{iso-twist}, to conclude the proof it suffices to check that $\phi_{\alpha}(\rho_1\rho_2) = \phi_{\alpha}(\rho_1)\phi_{\alpha\beta}(\rho_2)$ for all $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \Gamma$, $\rho_1 \in \Delta(T)_{\beta} = \mathrm{Hom}_{T}(T(\beta^{-1}),T)$, and $\rho_2 \in \Delta(T)_{\gamma} = \mathrm{Hom}_{T}(T(\gamma^{-1}),T)$. Taking such $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\rho_1$, and $\rho_2$, we first recall that in the semigroup $\Delta(T)$ the product $\rho_1\rho_2$ is understood to be $\rho_1\mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}}(\rho_2)$ (see the proof of Proposition~\ref{delta-semi} for more details). Thus
\begin{align*}
\phi_{\alpha}(\rho_1\rho_2) & = \mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}f_{\alpha(\beta\gamma)}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_1\mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}}(\rho_2)) \\
& = \mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}f_{\alpha(\beta\gamma)}(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_1)\mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_2))\\
& = \mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\psi_{\alpha^{-1}}^{-1}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_1)\mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_2) \psi_{\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}})\\
& = \mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\psi_{\alpha^{-1}}^{-1}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_1)\psi_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}})\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\psi_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}^{-1} \mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_2) \psi_{\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}) \\
& = (\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}\mathcal{F}^{-1}f_{\alpha\beta}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_1))(\mathcal{T}_{\alpha} \mathcal{T}_{\alpha\beta}^{-1} \mathcal{T}_{\alpha\beta} \mathcal{F}^{-1}(f_{(\alpha\beta)\gamma} \mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}(\rho_2)))\\
& = \phi_{\alpha}(\rho_1)\mathcal{T}_{\alpha} \mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}\alpha^{-1}}\phi_{\alpha\beta}(\rho_2)\\
& = \phi_{\alpha}(\rho_1)\mathcal{T}_{\beta^{-1}}\phi_{\alpha\beta}(\rho_2) \\
& = \phi_{\alpha}(\rho_1)\phi_{\alpha\beta}(\rho_2), 
\end{align*}
as desired.

label: dom-rem
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{dom-rem}
Note that (T5) makes sense because if $\bm{d}(a)=\bm{r}(\tau_{\beta}(b))$, then 
\[\bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha\beta}(b)) = \tau_{\alpha\beta}(\bm{r}(b)) = \tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(\bm{r}(b)) = \tau_{\alpha}(\bm{d}(a)) = \bm{d}(\tau_{\alpha}(a)),\] 
using (T1)--(T4). Conversely, if $a,b \in \mathcal{G}$ are such that $\bm{d}(\tau_{\alpha}(a)) = \bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha\beta}(b))$, then 
\[\tau_{\alpha}(\bm{r}(\tau_{\beta}(b))) = \tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(\bm{r}(b))) = \tau_{\alpha\beta}(\bm{r}(b)) = \bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha\beta}(b)) = \bm{d}(\tau_{\alpha}(a)) = \tau_{\alpha}(\bm{d}(a)),\]
and so $\bm{d}(a) = \bm{r}(\tau_{\beta}(b))$, since $\tau_{\alpha}$ is bijective.
head: environment

label: p:tau.eps
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) First note that (T1)--(T2) imply that on $\mathcal G^0$, we have $\tau_\varepsilon\tau_\varepsilon=\tau_\varepsilon$, and hence $\tau_\varepsilon|_{\mathcal G^0} = 1_{\mathcal G^0}$.  Now let $a\in \mathcal G$.  Then 
\[\tau_\varepsilon^2(a) = \tau_\varepsilon(aa^{-1} \tau_\varepsilon(a))=\tau_\varepsilon(aa^{-1})\tau_\varepsilon(a) = aa^{-1} \tau_{\varepsilon}(a)=\tau_\varepsilon(a).\]  
Thus $\tau_\varepsilon(a) = a$.

\smallskip

(2) We compute for composable $a,b\in \mathcal G_\varepsilon$ that 
\[\tau_\alpha(ab) = \tau_\alpha(a\tau_\varepsilon(b)) = \tau_\alpha(a)\tau_\alpha(b),\] by (1) and (T5).

label: gp-twist-thrm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{gp-twist-thrm}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $\mathcal{G}$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded ample groupoid, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $\mathcal{G}$. Then $\mathcal G^\tau$ is a $\, \Gamma$-graded ample groupoid, with the same grading as $\mathcal{G}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiplication is continuous being the composition 
\[(a,b)\mapsto (a,|a|,b)\mapsto (a,\tau_{|a|}(b))\mapsto a\tau_{|a|}(b)\] 
of continuous maps. 
    
If $a\in \mathcal G_\alpha$ and $b\in \mathcal G_\beta$, then $a\ast b=a\tau_\alpha(b)\in \mathcal G_{\alpha\beta}$, and so 
\[\bm{d}^\tau(a\ast b) = \tau_{(\alpha\beta)^{-1}}(\bm{d}(a\tau_\alpha(b))) = \tau_{(\alpha\beta)^{-1}}\tau_\alpha(\bm{d}(b)) = \tau_{\beta^{-1}}(\bm{d}(b)) = \bm{d}^{\tau}(b)\] 
using (T1)--(T3).  Also $\bm{r}^\tau(a\ast b) = \bm{r}(a\tau_\alpha(b))=\bm{r}^\tau(a)$.  
    
We next check associativity. Suppose that $a\in \mathcal G_\alpha$, $b\in \mathcal G_\beta$, and $c\in \mathcal G_\gamma$, where $a,b$ and $b,c$ are composable in $\mathcal G^\tau$. In particular, $\tau_{\beta^{-1}}(\bm{d}(b))=\bm{r}(c)$, and so $\bm{d}(b) = \bm{r}(\tau_\beta(c))$ by (T1)--(T4).  Then we compute
\begin{align*}
(a\ast b)\ast c &= (a\tau_\alpha(b))\tau_{\alpha\beta}(c)\\ 
a\ast(b\ast c) &= a\tau_\alpha(b\tau_\beta(c))
\end{align*}
and associativity follows from (T5).

Next we check that $\mathcal G^\tau$ is a category, by making sure $\bm{r}^\tau(a)\ast a=a$ and $a\ast \bm{d}^\tau(a)=a$.  So, let $a\in \mathcal G_\alpha$.  Then 
\[\bm{r}^\tau(a)\ast a = \bm{r}(a)\tau_\varepsilon(a) = \bm{r}(a)a=a,\] 
by Lemma~\ref{p:tau.eps}(1).  On the other hand, 
\[a\ast \bm{d}^{\tau}(a)= a \tau_\alpha(\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(\bm{d}(a))) = a\bm{d}(a)=a,\] 
using (T1)--(T2).

Note that $\mathcal G^\tau\to \Gamma$, $a\mapsto |a|$, is a grading on $\mathcal G^\tau$, as $|a\ast b| = |a||\tau_{|a|}(b)| = |a||b|$.

Finally, we claim that the inverse of $a\in \mathcal G_\alpha$ in $\mathcal G^\tau$ is given by $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a^{-1})=\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)^{-1}$.  Indeed, 
\[\bm{r}^{\tau}(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a^{-1})) = \bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a^{-1})) = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(\bm{d}(a)) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(\bm{d}(a)) = \bm{d}^{\tau}(a).\] 
We then compute $a\ast \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a^{-1}) = aa^{-1} = \bm{r}^{\tau}(a)$. Thus $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a^{-1})$ is a right inverse to $a$.  On the other hand, $\bm{d}^{\tau}(\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)^{-1}) = \bm{r}(a)$, and we have 
\[\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)^{-1}\ast a = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a) = \bm{d}(\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)) =\bm{d}^{\tau}(a).\]    
In particular, it follows the inversion is continuous, as it is the composition $a\mapsto (|a|^{-1},a)\mapsto \tau_{|a|^{-1}}(a)^{-1}$ of continuous maps.
head: environment

label: c:inverse.gpd.twist
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{c:inverse.gpd.twist}
The inverse in $\mathcal G^\tau$ is given on $a\in \mathcal G_{\alpha}$ by $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a^{-1})=\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)^{-1}$.

label: groupoid-alg-twist
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{groupoid-alg-twist}
As with semigroups, we can construct \emph{algebraic} Zhang twists on a groupoid, through homomorphisms to the graded automorphism group. (See Remark~\ref{alg-eg}.) 

Specifically, for a $\Gamma$-graded ample groupoid $\mathcal{G}$, let $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$ denote the group of graded homeomorphisms of $\mathcal{G}$, that are also functors. Now, suppose that $\tau : \Gamma \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$ is a homomorphism, and let $\tau_{\alpha} := \tau(\alpha)$ for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Then for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $a \in \mathcal{G}_{\beta}$, and $b \in \mathcal{G}$ such that $\bm{d}(a)=\bm{r}(\tau_\beta(b))$, we have 
\[\tau_\alpha(a\tau_\beta(b)) = \tau_\alpha(a)\tau_\alpha(\tau_\beta(b)) = \tau_\alpha(a)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(b),\]
which shows that $\{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ satisfies (T5). It is clear that (T1)--(T4) are satisfied as well.

If $\Gamma = \mathbb Z$, then, as in Remark~\ref{aut-eg}, we can construct an algebraic Zhang twist $\{\psi^n \mid n \in \mathbb Z\}$ on $\mathcal{G}$, from any graded automorphism $\psi : \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{G}$.

label: slice-lem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{slice-lem}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $\mathcal{G}$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded ample groupoid, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $\mathcal{G}$. Then $\, \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau})$ as sets.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $U\subseteq\mathcal{G}$. Since $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}$ is a bijection, and $\bm{d}^{\tau}|_U =\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}\circ \bm{d}|_U$, we conclude that $\bm{d}|_U$ is injective if and only if $\bm{d}^{\tau}|_U$ is injective. Also, $\bm{r}^\tau|_U = \bm{r}|_U$, and hence either both are injective or neither. Since the topologies and gradings on $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{G}^{\tau}$ coincide (see Theorem~\ref{gp-twist-thrm}), we conclude that $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau})$.

label: groupoid-semigp-prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{groupoid-semigp-prop}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $\mathcal{G}$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded ample groupoid, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $\mathcal{G}$. For each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ define $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} : \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}) \to \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$ by $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U) := \tau_{\alpha}(U)$. Then $\overline{\tau} :=\{\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a semi-algebraic Zhang twist on $\, \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$, and $\, \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})^{\overline{\tau}}$ as semigroups.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $\alpha \in \Gamma$, since $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a graded homeomorphism, it induces a bijection on the set of homogeneous compact open subsets of $\mathcal{G}$. It then follows from (T3)--(T4) that $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} : \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}) \to \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$ is a graded bijection. Now let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $U \in \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})_{\beta}$, and $V \in \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$. Then, using (T5) and Remark~\ref{dom-rem},
\begin{align*}
\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(V)) & = \{\tau_{\alpha}(a\tau_{\beta}(b)) \mid a \in U, b \in V,  \bm{d}(a)=\bm{r}(\tau_{\beta}(b)) \big\}\\ 
& = \{\tau_{\alpha}(a)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(b) \mid a \in U, b \in V,  \bm{d}(\tau_{\alpha}(a))=\bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha\beta}(b)) \big\}\\ 
& = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U)\overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(V).
\end{align*}
Hence $\overline{\tau}$ is a Zhang twist on $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$.

It is easy to see that $E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$ consists of compact open subsets of $\mathcal{G}^{0}$. So, using (T1)--(T2), for any $U \in E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$ we have $\tau_{\varepsilon} (\tau_{\varepsilon} (U)) = \tau_{\varepsilon}(U)$. Since $\tau_{\varepsilon}$ is a bijection, this means that $\overline{\tau}_{\varepsilon}(U) = \tau_{\varepsilon} (U) = U$. Hence $\overline{\tau}$ restricts to a Zhang twist on $E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}. Also, using Corollary~\ref{c:inverse.gpd.twist},
\[\overline{\tau}_{\alpha^{-1}}(U)^{-1} = \{\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(a)^{-1} \mid a \in U \big\}  = \{\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a) \mid a \in U^{-1} \big\} = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}^{-1}(U^{-1})\]
for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$ and $U \in \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$. Now, let $E: = E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$, $\alpha \in \Gamma$, and $U, V \in E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$. Then, using Lemma~\ref{p:tau.eps}(2), we have
\begin{align*}
\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}|_E(UV) & = \{\tau_{\alpha}(ab) \mid a \in U, b \in V,  \bm{d}(a)=\bm{r}(b) \big\}\\ 
& = \{\tau_{\alpha}(a)\tau_{\alpha}(b) \mid a \in U, b \in V,  \bm{d}(\tau_{\alpha}(a))=\bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha}(b)) \big\}\\ 
& = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}|_E(U)\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}|_E(V),
\end{align*}
and so $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}|_E$ is a semigroup homomorphism. Finally, using (T2), for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, and $U \in E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$, gives $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}|_E(\overline{\tau}_{\beta}|_E(U)) = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}|_E(U)$. Hence $\{\tau_{\alpha}|_{E(S)} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is an algebraic Zhang twist on $E(\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}))$, and so $\overline{\tau}$ is a semi-algebraic Zhang twist on $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})$.

By Lemma~\ref{slice-lem}, $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})^{\overline{\tau}}$ as sets, and so for the final claim it suffices to show that the multiplication operations on $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau})$ and $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})^{\overline{\tau}}$ coincide. Let $U,V \in \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})^{\overline{\tau}}$, with $U \subseteq \mathcal{G}_{\alpha}$. Then in $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau})$,
\begin{align*}
UV&= \{a*b \mid a \in U, b \in V, \bm{d}^{\tau}(a) =\bm{r}^{\tau}(b)\} \\ 
& = \{a\tau_{\alpha}(b) \mid a \in U, b \in V, \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(\bm{d}(a))=\bm{r}(b)\}\\
& = \{a\tau_{\alpha}(b) \mid a \in U, b \in V, \bm{d}(a)=\bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha}(b))\},
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from (T4) and the fact that $\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}|_{\mathcal G^0} = \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}|_{\mathcal G^0}$, by (T2). On the other hand, in $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})^{\overline{\tau}}$,
\[U*V = U\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(V) = \{a\tau_{\alpha}(b) \mid a \in U, b \in V,  \bm{d}(a)=\bm{r}(\tau_{\alpha}(b)) \big\}.\]
Hence the multiplication operations on $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G}^{\tau})$ and $\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}^{\operatorname{gr}}(\mathcal{G})^{\overline{\tau}}$ agree.

label: semigp-groupoid-prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{semigp-groupoid-prop}
Let $\, \Gamma$ be a group, $S$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded-Boolean inverse $\land$-semigroup, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a semi-algebraic Zhang twist on $S$. For each $\alpha \in \Gamma$ define $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} : \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S) \to \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$ by $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U) := \tau_{\alpha}(U)$. Then $\overline{\tau} :=\{\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is a Zhang twist on $\, \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$, and $\, \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$ as groupoids.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{twist-id-elt}(4), $\tau_{\varepsilon}(s) = s$ for all $s \in S$, and so we can apply Lemma~\ref{npt}(4), to conclude that each $\tau_{\alpha}$ is an order-isomorphism on $S$, and therefore takes each ultrafilter on $S$ to an ultrafilter, as does $\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}$. Thus the function $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} : \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S) \to \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$ is well-defined, for each $\alpha \in \Gamma$. Since each $\tau_{\alpha}$ is a graded bijection, so is $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}$.

The topology on $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$ is generated by basic open sets of the form 
\[\mathcal{Y}_s := \{U \in \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S) \mid s \in U\},\] 
where $s \in S$--see \cite[Lemma 5.6]{RZ2}. We have $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}^{-1}(\mathcal{Y}_s) = \mathcal{Y}_{\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(s)}$ and $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{Y}_s) = \mathcal{Y}_{\tau_{\alpha}(s)}$, for all $\alpha \in \Gamma$ and $s \in S$, and so $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}$ is a homeomorphism.

By~\cite[Lemma 2.8(2)]{Lawson3}, an ultrafilter on $S$ belongs to $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^0$ if and only if it contains an idempotent. Since each $\tau_{\alpha}$ preserves $E(S)$ (see Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}), it follows that $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}$ satisfies (T1).

To verify (T2), let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $U \in \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$, and $r,s \in U$. Since $U$ is downward directed, we can find $t \in U$ such that $t\leq r$ and $t \leq s$. Write $t = ru$ for some $u \in E(S)$. Then $r^{-1}t = r^{-1}ru \in E(S)$, and so, given that $\tau$ is semi-algebraic, $\tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(r^{-1}t)) = \tau_{\alpha\beta}(r^{-1}t)$. Since $r^{-1}t \leq r^{-1}s$, and $\tau_{\alpha\beta}$ is an order-isomorphism, we have $\tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(r^{-1}t)) \leq \tau_{\alpha\beta}(r^{-1}s)$. Therefore 
\[\tau_{\alpha\beta}(r^{-1}s) \in \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(U^{-1}U))^{\uparrow} = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(U^{-1} \cdot U)).\]
So $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(U^{-1}U) \subseteq \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(U^{-1}\cdot U))$, which implies that $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(U^{-1} \cdot U) \subseteq \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(U^{-1}\cdot U))$. Likewise $\tau_{\alpha\beta}(r^{-1}t) \leq \tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(r^{-1}s))$ implies that $\tau_{\alpha}(\tau_{\beta}(r^{-1}s)) \in \overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(U^{-1} \cdot U)$, and therefore $\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(U^{-1}\cdot U)) = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(U^{-1} \cdot U)$.

For (T3), let $\alpha \in \Gamma$, $U \in \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$, and $r,s \in U$. Then, as above, there exists $t \in U$ such that $t\leq r$ and $t \leq s$. Hence also $t^{-1} \leq s^{-1}$, and therefore $t^{-1}t \leq t^{-1}r \leq s^{-1}r$. By hypothesis on $\tau$, Proposition~\ref{inverse-twist}(1), and Lemma~\ref{npt}(5),
\[\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(t) = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}^{-1}(t^{-1})\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}^{-1}(t^{-1})^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha^{-1}}^{-1}(t^{-1}t) = \tau_{\alpha}(t^{-1}t)^{-1} = \tau_{\alpha}(t^{-1}t),\]
where the last equality follows from the fact that $\tau_{\alpha}(t^{-1}t) \in E(S)$, by Lemma~\ref{idempt-lem}. Thus
\[\tau_{\alpha}(s^{-1}r) \geq \tau_{\alpha}(t^{-1}t) = \tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(t),\]
and so
\[\overline{\tau}_{\alpha} \circ \bm{d}(U) = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U^{-1} \cdot U) = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U^{-1} U)^{\uparrow} \subseteq (\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U)^{-1} \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U))^{\uparrow} = \bm{d} \circ \overline{\tau}_{\alpha} (U).\]
Likewise
\[\tau_{\alpha}(s)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(r) \geq \tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(t) = \tau_{\alpha}(t^{-1}t),\] 
and hence
\[\bm{d} \circ \overline{\tau}_{\alpha} (U) = (\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U)^{-1} \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U))^{\uparrow} \subseteq \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U^{-1} U)^{\uparrow} = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha} \circ \bm{d}(U).\]
Thus $\bm{d} \circ \overline{\tau}_{\alpha} = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha} \circ \bm{d}$.

The verification of (T4) is entirely analogous to that of (T3), but using the identity $\tau_{\alpha}(tt^{-1}) = \tau_{\alpha}(t)\tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}$ (see Lemma~\ref{npt}(5)) in place of $\tau_{\alpha}(t^{-1}t) = \tau_{\alpha}(t)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha}(t)$.

To check (T5), let $\alpha, \beta \in \Gamma$, $U \in \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)_{\beta}$, and $V \in \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)$ be such that $\bm{d}(U) = \bm{r}(\tau_{\beta}(V))$. Then
\begin{align*}
\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U \cdot \overline{\tau}_{\beta}(V)) = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U\overline{\tau}_{\beta}(V))^{\uparrow} & = \{\tau_{\alpha}(s \tau_{\beta}(t)) \mid s \in U, t \in V\}^{\uparrow}\\
& = \{\tau_{\alpha}(s) \tau_{\alpha\beta}(t) \mid s \in U, t \in V\}^{\uparrow}\\
& = (\overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U)\overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(V))^{\uparrow} = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(U) \cdot \overline{\tau}_{\alpha\beta}(V).
\end{align*}

Finally, by Lemma~\ref{npt}(3), the ultrafilters on $S$ and $S^{\tau}$ coincide, and so $ \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S) = \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$ as sets. Now, let $U,V \in \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau}) = \operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$, and let $\alpha := |U|$ and $\beta := |V|$. Then in $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau})$, using Lemma~\ref{npt}(1) and the hypothesis on $\tau$,
\[\bm{d}(U) = \{\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s)^{-1}*t \mid s,t \in U\}^{\uparrow} = \{\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(t) \mid s,t \in U\}^{\uparrow},\]
and
\[\bm{r}(V) = \{p*\tau_{\beta}^{-1}(r^{-1}) \mid p,r \in V\}^{\uparrow} = \{p\tau_{\beta}(\tau_{\beta}^{-1}(r^{-1})) \mid p,r \in V\}^{\uparrow} = \{pr^{-1} \mid p,r \in V\}^{\uparrow},\]
while in $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$, using Corollary~\ref{c:inverse.gpd.twist},
\[\bm{d}^{\overline{\tau}}(U) = \overline{\tau}_{\alpha^{-1}}(U)^{-1} * U = (\overline{\tau}_{\alpha^{-1}}(U)^{-1}\overline{\tau}_{\alpha^{-1}}(U))^{\uparrow} = \{\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(s)^{-1}\tau_{\alpha^{-1}}(t) \mid s,t \in U\}^{\uparrow},\]
and
\[\bm{r}^{\overline{\tau}}(V) = \{pr^{-1} \mid p,r \in V\}^{\uparrow}.\]
Thus the unit spaces of $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau})$ and $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$ coincide, and $U$ and $V$ are composable in $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau})$ if and only if they are composable in $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$. So to conclude the proof it suffices to suppose that $U$ and $V$ are composable, and show that their products in $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau})$ and $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$ agree. In $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S^{\tau})$ we have
\[U \cdot V = \{s*t \mid s \in U, t \in V\}^{\uparrow} = \{s\tau_{\alpha}(t) \mid s \in U, t \in V\}^{\uparrow},\]
while in $\operatorname{\mathsf{G}}(S)^{\overline{\tau}}$,
\[U*V = U \cdot \overline{\tau}_{\alpha}(V) = \{s\tau_{\alpha}(t) \mid s \in U, t \in V\}^{\uparrow}.\]
Thus $U \cdot V = U*V$, as claimed.

label: p:gpd.alg.twist
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{p:gpd.alg.twist}
Let $K$ be a commutative unital ring, $\, \Gamma$ a group, $\mathcal{G}$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded ample groupoid, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $\mathcal{G}$. If $f\in K\mathcal G_{\beta}$ and $g\in K\mathcal G_{\gamma}$, then $\tau_{\alpha}(f\tau_{\beta}(g)) = \tau_{\alpha}(f)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ for all $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first compute 
\[\tau_{\alpha}(f\tau_{\beta}(g))(a) = \sum_{bc=\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(a)}f(b)g(\tau_{\beta}^{-1}(c))=\sum_{\tau_{\alpha}(bc)=a}f(b)g(\tau_{\beta}^{-1}(c)).\]
Putting $d:=\tau_{\beta}^{-1}(c)$, and using that $f(b)\neq 0$ implies $b\in \mathcal G_{\beta}$, we can rewrite this as
\[\sum_{\tau_{\alpha}(b\tau_{\beta}(d))=a}f(b)g(d)=\sum_{\tau_{\alpha}(b)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(d)=a}f(b)g(d).\] 
Now letting $x:=\tau_{\alpha}(b)$ and $y:= \tau_{\alpha\beta}(d)$, we can rewrite the last expression as
\[\sum_{xy=a}f(\tau_{\alpha}^{-1}(x))g(\tau_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}(y)) = \sum_{xy=a}\tau_{\alpha}(f)(x)\tau_{\alpha\beta}(g)(y) =(\tau_{\alpha}(f) \tau_{\alpha\beta}(g))(a),\]
as required.

label: groupoid-algebra-thrm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{groupoid-algebra-thrm}
Let $K$ be a commutative unital ring, $\, \Gamma$ a group, $\mathcal{G}$ a $\, \Gamma$-graded ample groupoid, and $\tau = \{\tau_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ a Zhang twist on $\mathcal{G}$. Let $\tau$ also denote the associated Zhang twist on $K\mathcal G$, given by $\tau_{\alpha}(f) := f\circ \tau_{\alpha}^{-1}$. Then $K\mathcal{G}^{\tau} = (K\mathcal{G})^{\tau}$ as $K$-algebras.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By construction, $K\mathcal{G}^{\tau} = K\mathcal{G} = (K\mathcal{G})^{\tau}$ as $K$-modules.

Now let $f\in K\mathcal G_\beta$ and $g\in K\mathcal G_\gamma$.  Then their product in $K\mathcal G^\tau$ is given by
\[fg(a) = \sum_{b\ast c=a}f(b)g(c)=\sum_{b\tau_{\beta}(c)=a}f(b)g(c),\]
since $f(b)\neq 0$ implies $b\in \mathcal G_\beta$. Substituting $d:=\tau_\beta(c)$ yields
\[fg(a) = \sum_{bd=a}f(b)g(\tau_\beta^{-1}(d)) = \sum_{bd=a}f(b)\tau_\beta(g)(d) = (f\tau_\beta(g))(a)=f\ast g(a).\]
Hence $K\mathcal{G}^{\tau} = (K\mathcal{G})^{\tau}$ as $K$-algebras.

label: popfh77
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{popfh77}
Let $E$ be a finite directed graph without sinks, and $h$ an automorphism of $\, (E^\infty,T)$.  Then $\tau\colon \mathcal G_E\to \mathcal G_E$, given by $\tau(x,k,y) := (h(x),k,h(y))$, is a graded automorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The map $\tau$ is well-defined. Indeed,   if $k=m-n$ and $T^m(x)=T^n(y)$, then 
\[T^m(h(x)) = h(T^m(x)) = h(T^n(y)) = T^n(h(y)),\] 
and so $\tau(x,m-n,y) = (h(x),m-n,h(y))$ is in $\mathcal G_E$.  Clearly $\tau$ preserves the degree. It is immediate from the definitions that $\tau$ is a functor, as 
\[\tau((x,k,y)(y,\ell,z)) = (h(x), k+\ell,h(z)) =(h(x),k,h(y))(h(y), \ell, h(z)) = \tau(x,k,y)\tau(y,\ell,z).\]
    
Note that $\tau^{-1}$ is induced by the automorphism $h^{-1}$, as $\tau^{-1}(x,k,y) = (h^{-1}(x),k,h^{-1}(y))$. Continuity follows from the observation that 
\[\tau^{-1}(Z(U,(m,n),V)) = Z(h^{-1}(U),(m,n),h^{-1}(V)).\]
Note that 
\[T^m(h^{-1}(U)) = h^{-1} (T^m(U)) = h^{-1} (T^n(V)) = T^n(h^{-1}(V)).\] 
Also $T|_{h^{-1} (U)}$ is injective, as $(T\circ h^{-1})|_U = h^{-1}\circ T|_U$, and similarly for $V$.

label: shift-eg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{shift-eg}
Let $E=(E^0,E^1,\mathbf{r},\mathbf{s})$ be a directed graph, where $E^0 = \{v\}$, and $E^1$ has at least $3$ elements. Let $x$ be a path in $E$, that, viewed as a word in the elements of $E^1$, does not overlap itself--that is, no nonempty prefix of $x$ is also a suffix. Let $\sigma\colon E^1 \to E^1$ be any permutation fixing the first and last letter of $x$. Define $h_{\sigma,x}\colon E^\infty\to E^\infty$ so that $h_{\sigma,x}(z)$ coincides with $z \in E^\infty$, except that the letter immediately before each occurrence of $x$ in $z$ is replaced by $\sigma$ of that letter. Because occurrences of $x$ do not overlap, and because consecutive occurrences $xx$ are fixed, as $\sigma$ fixes the last letter of $x$, it is easy to see that $h_{\sigma,x}$ is an automorphism, with the same order as $\sigma$.
